opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a real chance progress slows down, and it's worth taking that seriously rather than just extrapolating straight lines forever.

The main way I think about it is to break down what's actually been driving progress. A huge fraction of recent gains has come from scaling up compute: more chips, bigger training runs, more money. Then on top of that you have algorithmic progress, which has been substantial, and more recently a lot of gains from post-training, reinforcement learning, and inference-time compute. The question is how long each of those inputs can keep growing at the current rate.

On compute, there are pretty clear limits on how long you can keep scaling spending by something like 3 to 5x per year. At some point you're talking about training runs that cost a meaningful fraction of what the largest companies can spend, and then you run into constraints on power, on fab capacity, on just how much capital investors are willing to put in. My rough sense is that the current pace of compute scaling can continue for a few more years, maybe until somewhere around the end of the decade, and after that it probably has to slow unless AI is already generating enormous revenue that justifies much bigger investments.

So one way of putting it is that we're in a regime where either AI gets very powerful relatively soon, within the window where we can keep scaling inputs quickly, or progress slows down noticeably because those inputs stop growing as fast. That makes my probability mass kind of front-loaded. If we get through, say, 2030 without something like AI that can automate most AI research, I'd update toward longer timelines, because the easy scaling will have been used up and you're relying more on slower-moving algorithmic progress.

There are also other reasons for slowdown people point to. One is data: running out of high-quality human text. I think that's somewhat real but less binding than people sometimes say, because RL and synthetic data can substitute to some extent. Another is that the new paradigms, like RL on verifiable tasks, might work well in domains with clear feedback but generalize less well to messy, long-horizon real-world tasks. That's an empirical question I'm genuinely uncertain about.

Then there's the flip side: if AI starts meaningfully accelerating AI research itself, that could more than offset slowing compute growth. So it's not just "will inputs slow," it's also "do we hit the point where AI is speeding up its own development before they slow."

Putting that together, I'd say there's a substantial probability, maybe something like a third or more, that we see a meaningful slowdown in the underlying rate of progress over the next five or so years. But I wouldn't treat that as the default, and I think it's a mistake to plan only for the slow world, because the fast world is where a lot of the risk is concentrated and where preparation matters most.

r001.rationale: The response discusses a fast-progress scenario and concentrated risk, but does not say AI risks could arrive faster than government response times without AI automating its own development.

r002.rationale: It identifies spending limits as a plausible constraint: training runs could consume a meaningful share of major companies’ budgets, and continued scaling depends on AI generating enough revenue to justify larger investments.

r003.rationale: It describes algorithmic progress as slower-moving than scaling, but does not state that algorithmic progress itself would slow if compute stopped growing.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think there's a real chance of this, and I want to be careful to separate a few different things that could be going on.

The first thing I'd say is that a lot of the progress we've seen over the past several years has come from scaling up compute very rapidly. Training compute for frontier models has been growing something like 4 or 5x per year, and that's been driven by spending going up, chips getting better, and labs building out larger and larger clusters. That rate of compute scaling just can't continue indefinitely. At some point you run into the fraction of world GDP that people are willing to spend on this, you run into power constraints, chip fab capacity, that sort of thing. My guess is that around 2028 to 2030 or so, if we haven't gotten to very powerful AI by then, you'd expect compute scaling to slow down substantially, maybe to something more like the historical hardware improvement rate rather than this very aggressive investment-driven ramp.

And if compute scaling slows, I'd expect progress to slow too. Not to zero, because there's also algorithmic progress, which has been contributing a comparable amount — maybe the effective compute from algorithms has also been improving several-fold per year. But I think some of that algorithmic progress is itself downstream of having more compute to run experiments with, and it's also downstream of the labor force working on this growing very quickly, which also can't keep growing at the current rate forever.

So the picture I have is something like: there's a window, maybe the next five years or so, where the current trends roughly continue. And if we get to AI systems that can substantially automate AI research within that window, then I think things probably accelerate rather than slow down, because you've substituted in a much faster-growing input. But if we don't get there in that window, then I think the base rates shift pretty substantially toward slower progress, and timelines get a lot longer and a lot more uncertain. My probability on getting to that kind of system by the end of the decade is maybe somewhere in the range of 25 to 50 percent — I go back and forth — but conditional on missing that, I'd put a lot of weight on it taking quite a bit longer.

The other thing I'd flag is that there's a separate question of whether the current paradigm hits some kind of wall, where additional scale just doesn't buy you the capabilities you care about. I'm somewhat skeptical of hard-wall stories, mostly because we've seen a bunch of them predicted and then not pan out, but I don't think they're crazy. The thing I'd be looking for is whether progress on things like long-horizon agency and the ability to do long, messy research tasks keeps tracking the scaling trends, because that's the capability that actually matters for the feedback loop. If that starts to lag, that's a meaningful update toward slowdown for me.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible slowdown and AI research automation, but does not say that default AI progress could bring risks quickly relative to government response times.

r002.rationale: It identifies a limit on how much people would spend on AI as one constraint on continued compute scaling.

r003.rationale: It says some algorithmic progress depends on having more compute for experiments, indicating that this progress would slow if compute stopped growing.

astra-6.text:
I think there’s a substantial chance that progress slows down, but it’s useful to distinguish a few different things that could mean. One is that scaling up pretraining stops delivering improvements at the rate we’ve seen. Another is that AI systems stop getting more useful overall. The first could happen without the second, because you could still get substantial improvements from better algorithms, post-training, or spending more compute when the model is solving a problem.

The question I’d focus on is how hard it is to turn additional resources into additional capability. If progress requires increasingly large training runs, then eventually you run into constraints on how much money people are willing to spend and how quickly they can build the infrastructure. That gives you a fairly natural reason to expect some slowdown. But it doesn’t tell you where that slowdown happens relative to systems being able to automate a lot of economically valuable work.

And AI doing AI research could change that picture quite substantially. You don’t need it to completely automate research for it to accelerate progress; making researchers more productive could already matter. On the other hand, if the bottlenecks are experiments that take a long time or access to compute, having more capable research assistants might help less than you’d initially expect.

So I’d put meaningful probability on a slowdown. I just wouldn’t treat it as something we can confidently count on, especially before AI reaches capabilities that would have very large consequences.

r001.rationale: The response discusses possible slowdown and AI research assistance, but does not say AI risks could arrive quickly relative to government response times without AI development automation.

r002.rationale: It identifies limits on how much money people are willing to spend on increasingly large training runs as a reason progress could slow, communicating a spending ceiling.

r003.rationale: It says better algorithms could improve capabilities even if pretraining scaling slows; it does not say algorithmic progress would also slow if compute stopped growing.

sol-6.1.text:
I think there’s a substantial chance that progress slows down, but I wouldn’t want to count on it. It’s useful to distinguish between progress slowing because we stop putting in more resources and progress slowing because additional resources stop buying us as much capability.

You could imagine scaling becoming less effective, or running into difficulties with data, or finding that systems which look impressive on benchmarks still struggle to do useful work reliably. Those would all be reasons to update toward slower progress. But there are also multiple ways to keep making progress: better algorithms, more compute, and using AI systems to help with research.

The last one seems particularly important. If AI gets good enough to substantially accelerate AI research, then a slowdown in some existing approach might not translate into a slowdown overall. You could have systems helping find the next approach.

So I’d put meaningful probability on a slowdown, including one that lasts a while. But for decisions about safety, the question isn’t just what trajectory is most likely. It’s whether the probability of rapid progress is large enough that we should prepare for it. And I think it is.

r001.rationale: The response says rapid progress is plausible enough to prepare for, but does not compare progress with government response times or state that this could happen without AI-assisted development.

r002.rationale: It mentions progress slowing if more resources stop being added, but does not identify a ceiling on economically justified compute spending.

r003.rationale: It names better algorithms as another route to progress, but does not say algorithmic progress would slow if compute stopped growing.
